papers.title: An end-to-end in silico framework for truth-based validation and regression testing of clinical genome sequencing pipelines, from simulated reads to reportable findings
papers.abstract: Clinical genome sequencing pipelines change often, and each change requires proportionate revalidation. Guidelines accept in silico data as a supplement but leave variant interpretation outside pipeline validation, and, to our knowledge, no framework tests a pipeline against a known truth up to the reportable finding, so report specificity is not measured. We present a source-available framework that tests a pipeline end to end, from sequencing reads to the report, against a truth fixed before any run. It plants expert-curated pathogenic and benign variants from the same genes, and optionally synthetic variants that no database holds, into the GIAB HG002 germline background and records the expected class and report decision of each variant. It then simulates reads and runs secondary and tertiary analysis as black boxes through exchangeable adapters. Findings are compared with the truth at the call-set and report levels, each failure is assigned to the first pipeline stage where it appears, and a variant-by-variant comparison of two runs serves as a regression test. We applied the framework to nf-core/sarek with DeepVariant and to the ACMG/AMP classifier BIAS-2015, using 243 ClinGen-curated variants in five test sets. Single-nucleotide variant recall against the HG002 benchmark was 99.5% on simulated and 99.3% on real reads, and every planted variant was present in the reads and called with the correct genotype. The report included 115 of 117 pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants (98.3%) but withheld only 106 of 126 variants that must not be reported (84.1%), mainly because variants of uncertain significance were upgraded and recessive carriers were reported. Without ClinVar-derived criteria, report sensitivity fell to 74.4%. Most false reports of one test set came from diploid calling of the male chromosome X, and haploid calling removed them without side effects. In supplementary experiments, indels were called completely up to 20 bp, and BIAS-2015 left 74% of synthetic loss-of-function variants unreported because it combined criteria by the 2015 rules. The framework measures report-level sensitivity and specificity and localizes regressions, so it can supplement validation on human samples and support change control.

papers.title: The Segmentome: a novel representation of the DNA methylome identified by a Bayesian HMM framework
papers.abstract: Motivation: DNA methylation is organized along the genome into regions of relatively stable methylation (i.e. fully methylated or fully unmethylated regions), separated by transition zones. Differences in the boundaries of these methylation zones across cells can result from various regulatory and epigenetic mechanisms. Most DNA methylome studies, however, are focused on the detection of differentially methylated regions (DMRs), and this organization within a single methylome remains under explored. Furthermore it is unclear whether a segment-level descriptor can capture cell identity. Results: We introduce the segmentome, a segment-level representation of the methylome, and an unsupervised Bayesian hidden Markov model that infers it from WGBS data without predefined methylation thresholds or labels. The model combines CpG methylation levels with read-pattern entropy, local CpG correlation and CpG count to divide the genome into unmethylated, methylated and transition zones, the last characterized by heterogeneous read patterns. Applied to 207 samples of 39 human cell types, segmentome profiles grouped samples by cell type in an unsupervised manner (adjusted Rand index 0.55, adjusted mutual information 0.72). We next generated a segmentome atlas consisting of top segmentome biomarkers per human cell-type. These markers were capable of cell-of-origin determining in cell-free DNA and white blood cell samples. These results suggest that segmentation is a unique framework for analyzing DNA methylome.

papers.title: Layer-Specific Source-Anchored Transfer Learning for Multi-Omics Survival Prediction in Younger Breast Cancer Patients
papers.abstract: Background: Younger breast cancer patients ( =60, >=55, and >=50 years were used as the source to improve prediction in patients aged <50 years. LSAT-EN were evaluated in group-correlated simulations and in TCGA-BRCA integrating 6 omics layers. Binary survival at 2-4 years was assessed by AUC; censored survival by Harrell's C-index and 2-5-year inverse probability of censoring weighted (IPCW) AUC. Results: In simulation, LSAT-EN achieved the highest AUC under moderate source-target heterogeneity (sigma^2=0.25; 0.747- 0.802), outperforming GAS-EN (0.735-0.767), overall EN (0.683-0.710), individual EN (0.646-0.767), and glmtrans EN (0.640-0.733) across target training sample sizes (nT). Its advantage was greatest under higher source-target heterogeneity (sigma^2=4), particularly with small nT, where LSAT-EN achieved AUCs of 0.689- 0.789 compared with 0.590-0.771 across competing methods. In TCGA-BRCA data, LSAT-EN improved discrimination relative to overall and individual EN in all binary and Cox models across all time horizons and source age groups. The method also identified clinically/ biologically important mRNA and miRNA, as well as useful candidate miRNA-mRNA pairs, indicating powerful biomarker discovery capability. Conclusion: LSAT-EN is a powerful TL method for improving prediction for younger breast cancer patients; The framework may support prediction in other underrepresented populations with limited target-cohort data to advance cancer disparity ML research.

papers.title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
papers.abstract: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.

papers.title: GOParsimony: parsimonious saltation across the Gene Ontology digraph for efficient functional annotation
papers.abstract: Background. The Gene Ontology (GO) is standardly probed by biological researchers keen to discern the functional tendencies of their gene/protein data sets. However, lists of GO terms are often ontically overwhelming, and need to be filtered to remove redundancy. Methods for such filtering either employ predefined lists of terms that may not actually be relevant to a specific gene/protein set, or apply arbitrary thresholds, such as for semantic distance (i.e., GO term dissimilarity). Methods. Here, I introduce the tool GOParsimony, which is designed to avoid such issues and to pick out the most parsimonious (i.e., simplest, most concise) explanation for the functional tendencies of any set of proteins/genes. It achieves this by saltating across the GO digraph, assigning and updating cascades of term precedence until convergence. The set of GO terms assigned precedence = 1 is the most parsimonious set. Hierarchical clustering with other GO terms with higher precedence levels can be investigated for clues about functional modules. Results. GO term precedence graphs and two-dimensional heatmaps of GO terms and genes/proteins are output, along with other plots that can be cross-referenced for functional insights. In test analyses for five example data sets from budding yeast and human, GOParsimony consistently produces reduced GO term lists that have greater significance and low or intermediate coverage of the space of significant GO terms, when compared to other distributed methods in default mode. GOParsimony can be obtained at: https://github.com/pmharrison/GOParsimony .

papers.title: RAPTORGraph: graph-based pathway modeling for causal discovery in single-cell perturbations
papers.abstract: Experiments involving the perturbation of individual cells are central to understanding cellular mechanisms and can accelerate drug discovery. Causal representation learning allows us to uncover the latent factors that regulate biological systems and predict the impact of novel perturbations. Unfortunately, existing methods fail to address intervention spillover in a closed-world setting where intervention targets are known a priori, such as in Perturb-seq experiments, due to their reliance on dense encoders. Furthermore, incorporating curated biological pathways into the model imposes a confirmatory bias, forcing it to explain the data through preexisting pathways and reducing the set of hypotheses the model can explore, while discarding novel signals that lie outside the annotated pathways. In this work, we introduce RAPTORGraph, a {beta}-variational autoencoder with a GraphPathway encoder that explicitly models complex gene-to-gene interactions within learned pathways. Moreover, our model's preconditioning isolates the influence of perturbed genes, yielding clean, single-node latent interventions required for identifiable causal discovery and eliminating spillover. Finally, we train the model on data preprocessed with optimal-transport alignment, which guarantees a well-defined mapping between control and perturbed samples and further stabilizes the learned latent representations. We demonstrate that RAPTORGraph improves state-of-the-art performance on downstream analyses of unseen perturbations, such as non-additive interactions, while performing competitively on objective metrics, such as mean squared error and maximum mean discrepancy. The source code is available at https://github.com/sXperfect/RAPTORGraph.

papers.title: A trustworthy semantic knowledge network linking data-driven cell phenotypes to diseases and drugs
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association and other genetic studies have identified genes involved in disease pathogenesis, and their encoded proteins have provided therapeutic targets. However, little is known about which cells are the functional home of these disease-associated genes and proteins. Single-cell technologies are enabling high-resolution profiling of cell phenotypes and revealing cellular contexts of disease, yet much of the resulting knowledge remains embedded in individual datasets and scientific literature. To address these gaps, the National Library of Medicine has developed Cell Knowledge Network (NLM-CKN, https://nlm-ckn.org). Reproducible computational workflows have generated cell phenotype knowledge for 2,585 cell sets and 5,139 selectively expressed genes from 88 datasets covering 10 human organs. Mapping of these cell sets to cell types grounds Cell Ontology terms in experimental evidence. This experimental knowledge is integrated with external knowledge of anatomical and cell-type hierarchies, gene-disease associations, and therapeutic interventions. A semantic schema defines node types and relations, enabling knowledge to be transformed into triple assertions and loaded into an ArangoDB database with provenance and quantitative evidence. The NLM-CKN interface supports graphical exploration of the cellular constituents of healthy human tissues. Finally, topological analyses generate insights into cellular contributions to disease pathogenesis, cellular contexts for therapeutic intervention, and drug-repurposing hypotheses.

papers.title: Computational Analysis of Antioxidant Effects on Stress Response Mechanisms in Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Candida albicans was used as a eukaryotic model to study aging and oxidative stress response pathways focused on NAD dependent deacetylases, Sir2 and SIRT3. A significant gene expression regulation of both Sir2 and SIRT3 was observed under sublethal hydrogen peroxide treatment towards their association with stress adaptation. Natural ligands known for antioxidant properties were docked against Sir2 and SIRT3 structures. Binding free energy of most components fall in the range of -5.0 to -11 kcal/mol. The best candidates pterostilbene, quercetin and naringenin formed stable hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds within catalytic and NAD binding pockets confirmed by visualization. Detailed ADME profiling shows most of the ligands passed the Lipinski rule of five and revealed a very good gastrointestinal absorption. PASS (Prediction of Activity Spectra for Substances) and SOM (Sites of Metabolism) predicts antioxidants, anti-aging properties, toxicity profiles, with key metabolic hotspots. This integrated in-silico approach highlights naringenin and quercetin as promising modulators of Sir2/SIRT3 mediated metabolic pathways in Candida albicans, warranting further validation with the help of in-vitro and in-vivo methods.

papers.title: Stochastic gene expression drives state switching and phenotypic heterogeneity in RNA repair
papers.abstract: Bacterial populations often exhibit variability in cellular responses to antibiotics which can affect treatment success and survival outcomes. This heterogeneity suggests that genetically identical cells can occupy different states of susceptibility within the same population. Better understanding of these dynamic responses is essential for determining how cells respond to stress and survive antibiotic-induced damage. In this work, we investigate heterogeneity in antibiotic responses driven by the Rtc RNA repair system in E. coli. We develop a stochastic model of Rtc-mediated RNA repair to identify the drivers of heterogeneity at the single-cell level. We observe bimodality in cellular translational capacity and a transient memory in predicted responses to RNA damage, demonstrating how intrinsic stochasticity in Rtc-regulation can lead to phenotypic heterogeneity. Classifying single-cell trajectories, we predict drivers of state switching between the resistant and susceptible states, finding that stochastic expression of the rtc regulator determines entry into a resistant cell state, while dilution drives the system back into a susceptible state. These results indicate that heterogeneity in RNA repair emerges from stochastic switching between states, offering a route to understanding how individual cells survive in the presence of translation-targeting antibiotics.

papers.title: SPaRTA: Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis
papers.abstract: Spatial-omics technologies provide clinicians, pathologists, and biomedical researchers with high-resolution maps of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic activity within tissues. However, querying these complex datasets often requires specialized computational expertise, limiting their accessibility to domain experts without programming experience. In the current manuscript, we develop SPaRTA (Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis), a natural-language interface that translates free-text questions into executable spatial SQL queries over such data. We release SPaRTA-Bench, comprising dataset-specific database schemas, explicit query conventions, and 7,500 question-SQL pairs validated through LLM-assisted verification and targeted human review, spanning breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and melanoma tissue sections, and identify 15 failure modes in which a query runs but returns a wrong answer. Open-weight large language models (LLMs) of the Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and Phi families reach 10-40% execution accuracy zero-shot, and at most 61% with reasoning and execution feedback. Fine-tuning raises them to 63-77%, and they lose at most 6 percentage points on a tissue unseen in training. Execution feedback repairs queries that fail to run, but rarely queries that run and return a wrong answer.

papers.title: 2D U-NET Deep Learning Architecture for Atherosclerotic Lesion Segmentation and Quantification
papers.abstract: Mice are commonly used for experimental atherosclerosis research, and a common procedure involves morphometric analysis of atherosclerotic lesions on Oil Red O-stained cross-sections of the aortic root. However, manual measurement of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on numerous histological sections is tedious and time-consuming. Here, we developed a deep learning model based on convolutional neural network to quantify atherosclerotic lesions in cross-sectioned aortic roots of mice. Microscopy images were taken from cross-sectioned aortic roots of genetically diverse F2 mice derived from BALB/cJ and LP/J Apoe knockout mice and fed 12 weeks of a Western diet. Aortic cross-sections were stained with Oil Red O and hematoxylin and images captured. Atherosclerotic lesions were manually segmented in 2553 images using Zeiss AxioVision. These images were split into 1,533 for training the U-NET model, 510 for validation, and 510 images for testing. The developed model was evaluated for its performance to measure atherosclerotic lesions by comparing with manual measurement in test images. The model achieved a high degree of accuracy, with an F1 score of 0.82, a Jaccard score of 0.72, a Recall of 0.80, a precision of 0.87, and a correlation coefficient value of 0.98. While manual lesion measurement took approximately 5 minutes per image, the model performed the task in ~3.35 seconds, reducing measurement time by 98.9%. The developed 2D U-NET model provides a new platform for rapid and accurate quantification of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on Oil Red O-stained sections.

papers.title: Decision benchmarking of cryo-EM re-refinement
papers.abstract: Map fit is widely used in cryo-EM re-refinement. We benchmarked selection against retaining the deposited model (no operation), using packed-side-chain agreement with higher-resolution references. In a prespecified 3.0-3.6 [A] cohort (167 entries, 131 sequence groups), highest-correlation selection increased {chi}1 disagreement by 2.4{degrees} (95% interval 2.1-2.7{degrees}), with positive loss in 91% of groups. Group-weighted fractions with >20{degrees} increases and decreases were 7.2% and 3.7%; the fraction exceeding 1 [A] local side-chain RMSD rose by 2.4 percentage points. Selection by a half map withheld from re-refinement increased disagreement (2.29{degrees}; 1.70-2.97{degrees}; 99 entries). In 53 prespecified within-study low/high-resolution pairs, loss was 3.43{degrees} (2.85-4.02{degrees}), positive in 50 pairs; half-map loss was 2.35{degrees} (1.60-3.21{degrees}; 44 pairs). Primum provides fixed cohorts, residue sets and scoring tools to benchmark refiners and selection rules against no operation.

papers.title: Reference-Guided De Novo Retrieval of 3D Chromatin Organizational Features with Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Chromosome conformation maps reveal spatial genome organization through recurring contact patterns, some associated with established architectural features and others with less understood biological processes. Identifying instances of a pattern across these maps is necessary to investigate its biological associations and recurrence across experimental settings. However, conventional feature callers typically target predefined patterns, offering limited support when researchers can provide examples of a feature of interest but lack a dedicated detection method. We introduce Chromatin Fetch (C-Fetch), a reference-guided retrieval framework that uses examples of a desired feature and a contrasting class to rank and assign contact-map patches at provided candidate coordinates. C-Fetch learns a reusable representation through weakly KL-regularized 3D autoencoding of structurally related, non-temporal Hi-C and Micro-C patches without architectural feature labels. We demonstrate retrieval of biologically defined contacts, visually specified patterns, and established architectural features. Polycomb-guided retrieval identifies contacts enriched for PRC2-associated signals, exceeding enrichment from loop-guided assignments at 5 kb, while queries resembling condensed domains retrieve patches with progressively stronger rectangular enrichment at higher ranks. Loop-guided retrieval increases aggregate focal enrichment relative to complete Mustache proposal sets across four held-out maps, and selected contacts show greater focality loss after cohesin depletion than matched remaining candidates. Retrieval also extends to Region Capture Micro-C and HiChIP, with ranking agreement retained across biological replicates and reduced sequencing depths. Together, these results establish reference examples as a flexible means of specifying contact-map features of interest, enabling biological investigation, exploration of visual patterns, and refinement of existing calls across datasets and technologies.

papers.title: Cellular composition and the interpretation of candidate RNA readouts of trogocytosis in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Background: RNA measurements of genes associated with trogocytosis may reflect cellular composition rather than contact-dependent membrane acquisition. We evaluated an eight-gene candidate module in colorectal cancer (CRC) using expression- and lineage-matched random modules, independent compartment analysis and patient-level inference. A separate rare-transcript definition and cancer-model fitness screens provided complementary analyses. Results: In 62 GSE178341 patients, the module correlated with T-cell fraction ({rho}=0.767), but this association was typical of 10,000 matched modules (null median 0.766; one-sided empirical P=0.493; equal-tail two-sided P=0.985). A post hoc closest-10% matching sensitivity gave P=0.571. In 23 independent GSE132465 patients, the tumour-wide correlation was 0.735 (permutation P=0.00060) and the epithelial correlation was 0.376 (P=0.0892). The difference in absolute correlations was 0.359, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.041 to 0.759, leaving attenuation uncertain. Among 43,817 leukocytes, 16 CEACAM5-positive candidates arose from four patients; 15 had expression [≤]2 transcripts per million. Candidate counts were threshold-sensitive. No survival association was detected for the module in two cohorts. SCD fitness dependency reproduced across CRC organoids and cell lines, whereas adjusted SCD-VPS72 and exploratory ATF3-SMYD2 co-dependencies did not. Exploratory CH25H, ATF3 and FADS2 analyses yielded no Hallmark enrichment meeting the multiple-testing threshold. Conclusions: Matched-module calibration placed the strong association with T-cell abundance within the range expected for comparable immune-lineage genes. Independent compartment analysis was consistent with a contribution from cellular composition, although attenuation remained uncertain. These results identify the comparison conditions needed to interpret the tested RNA readouts. Linking them to membrane transfer requires event-resolved protein measurements.

papers.title: Resolving how genetic perturbations act through gene regulatory paths
papers.abstract: Perturb-seq measures transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic perturbations, but each gene's response mixes the contributions of many regulatory paths, so how a perturbation acts cannot be resolved from expression alone, however large the model. Here we present REGA-perturb, which supplies this missing information rather than adding model complexity: reference epigenomes define a scaffold of possible transcription factor (TF)-regulatory element-gene paths, and perturbation responses, pooled through shared latent programs, determine how each path is used, requiring only RNA measurements. Across three CRISPR interference screens totaling 2.4 million cells, REGA-perturb inferred TF-target relationships that agreed with ChIP-seq binding with a gain over random more than four times that of the best existing method, separated candidate direct from indirect targets, and predicted targets of TFs withheld from training. It also inferred perturbation-induced changes in TF activity not reflected in TF transcript levels, and resolved perturbation-specific regulatory rewiring in which opposing regulatory changes cancel at the expression level.

papers.title: Edi-Set-Flow: detecting differential RNA-editing at scale
papers.abstract: Background: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is a post-transcriptional modification catalysed by ADAR enzymes that can alter codons, splicing patterns, and RNA secondary structures. RNA editing is essential for innate immunity and nervous system development, and its dysregulation is implicated in neurological disorders, cancers, and autoimmune diseases. Despite its biological importance, accurately detecting RNA editing from RNA-seq data remains technically challenging, and robust inference of differential editing across experimental conditions is not straightforward. Findings: We have developed Edi-Set-Flow, a reproducible and scalable pipeline for transcriptome-wide A-to-I RNA editing analysis of bulk RNA-seq data. Implemented in Nextflow, the pipeline takes raw FASTQ files as input, trims reads and filters for quality, aligns reads to the reference genome, and identifies editing sites with JACUSA2. Common genetic variants are excluded using the gnomAD population database. Identified sites are annotated for genetic feature context and predicted functional consequences, and results are summarised in a user-friendly HTML report. The pipeline scales efficiently to hundreds or thousands of samples and is suitable for large datasets such as GTEx. An accompanying R package enables advanced analyses, including model fitting, hypothesis testing, false discovery rate control, and visualisation, thereby facilitating reliable statistical comparisons of editing across experimental groups. Applying Edi-Set-Flow to GTEx brain RNA-seq data, we uncovered distinct RNA editing signatures across brain tissues and recovered known protein-recoding events. Conclusions: Edi-Set-Flow provides researchers with a robust, user-friendly, scalable, end-to-end solution for efficiently identifying and interpreting biologically meaningful RNA editing events across diverse transcriptomic datasets, for both mouse and human.

papers.title: HYphlow: bringing end-to-end flow to HyPhy selection analyses, from taxon reconciliation to trait-based foreground assignment
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic analyses of molecular evolution often require repeated manual preparation to reconcile taxa, annotate trees, execute models, and summarize results. These steps become increasingly time-consuming and difficult to standardize as the number of taxa, genes, and analytical hypotheses increases. We present HYphlow, an open-source graphical workflow developed in Python that integrates data preparation, trait-based foreground branch assignment, HyPhy execution, and structured result extraction within a single interface. HYphlow reconciles taxon labels across alignments, trees, and trait data; reconstructs ancestral states using parsimony and maximum likelihood; generates alternative foreground annotations; executes HyPhy analyses locally or through portable scripts for high-performance computing; and records analytical decisions and settings throughout the workflow. We evaluated HYphlow using simulations and two published datasets comprising cryptochrome analyses in pigeons and doves and visual opsin analyses in skinks. A name-similarity threshold of 80 reliably recovered simulated spelling variants, while consensus foreground assignment increased precision relative to parsimony or maximum likelihood alone (0.928 vs 0.891 and 0.907, respectively), with a corresponding reduction in recall (0.875 vs 0.921 and 0.918). In the empirical datasets, HYphlow reconciled taxon labels, reconstructed or reproduced foreground hypotheses derived using different approaches, and generated selection results consistent with the principal conclusions of the original studies. HYphlow therefore provides a reproducible framework for carrying comparative molecular evolutionary analyses from independently prepared sequence, phylogenetic, and trait data through branch assignment, model execution, and results summary while retaining researcher control over analytical decisions. HYphlow is freely available under the MIT licence from GitHub at: https://github.com/Schott-Lab/HYphlow.

papers.title: GSET: Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories select compact contexts for mechanistic GRN inference
papers.abstract: Mechanistic inference of gene regulatory networks from temporal transcriptomic data can become computationally prohibitive at transcriptome scale, making gene selection an important determinant of which regulatory relationships can be recovered. However, gene selection for GRN inference commonly relies on static expression or co-expression structure, rather than prioritizing dynamically informative genes whose temporal patterns capture how transcriptional programs change and relate to one another. We introduce GSET (Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories), an upstream retrieval framework that extracts dynamic information from temporal gene embeddings using two complementary signals: an optimal transport residual, which captures gene-specific deviations from global embedding movement, and a KL divergence, which detects changes in local co-expression neighborhoods. Temporal gene-embedding similarity identifies static transcriptional programs, whereas vectorial GSET signals represent coordinated temporal changes among genes, complementing this static structure. Lagged comparisons of these signals further prioritize temporal relationships between programs and candidate bridge genes associated with their transitions. Integrated with CardamomOT, GSET combines static program cores with dynamically retrieved bridge genes into compact, program-informed gene sets for mechanistic GRN inference. In synthetic benchmarks, at equal gene budget these sets recover more of the regulatory links between programs than static selections of the same size, and inference on the edges within the set is comparable to that of the full-gene model on the same gene pairs. On a time course of mouse fibroblasts reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells, GSET traces the transition from the fibroblast program to the cell-cycle program. By providing a dynamic retrieval layer upstream of GRN inference, GSET nominates bridge genes as candidate regulators of cell-state transitions, which, once refined by a mechanistic model such as CardamomOT and confirmed by perturbation experiments, could open the way to controlling these transitions.

papers.title: The Reasoning Paradox in Scientific Sandboxes: Why Extended Reasoning Fails in Autonomous Bioinformatics and How to Fix It.
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) trained with extended reasoning, such as DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1, have established state-of-the-art benchmarks in formal logic, competitive programming, and mathematics. In interactive, empirical scientific sandboxes, however, their efficacy remains counter-intuitive. In the Bioinformatics Benchmark (BixBench), extended reasoning models paradoxically degraded in multi-turn environments, leading benchmark authors to exclude them from primary agentic evaluations. In this paper, we conduct the first systematic forensic audit of the internal cognitive monologue ( ... ) of open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) and matched instruction-tuned controls (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) deployed inside containerized computational biology sandboxes on Nvidia H100 GPUs. Our forensic analysis uncovers two distinct systemic failure modes: (1) The PubMed Prior Trap, in which reasoning models engage in epistemic rationalization within their cognitive stream, falsely convincing themselves that empirical datasets are missing and substituting empirical computation with speculative literature recall (e.g., estimating adjusted p-values based on "typical experimental outcomes"); and (2) Tag Language Nesting Collisions, in which models conflate agent-level XML action tags with Python syntax, producing terminal interpreter syntax errors. To resolve this paradox, we introduce Dual Track Decoupled Reasoning (DTDR), an agent scaffolding architecture that evicts internal cognitive monologues from multi-turn history, injects strict empirical grounding guardrails, and dynamically intercepts runtime tool invocations. On a stratified diagnostic benchmark spanning single-cell RNA-seq, bulk differential expression (DESeq2), and genomic variant prioritization (n=22 per arm), DTDR rescues the 14B reasoning model from 0.0% to 9.09% accuracy (2/22), doubling the performance of the matched non-reasoning coder control (4.55%, 1/22) while slashing code execution errors by 81% (13.6% vs. 72.7%) and reducing average steps to solution by 66% (1.77 vs. 5.18 steps). All replication pipelines, prompts, and trajectory manifests are openly released.

papers.title: Quantitative Donor Histology and Transcriptomics Link Pancreatic Composition and Precancers Across the Adult Lifespan
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) is the primary precursor to invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). While PanIN is common in the general population, PDAC is rare. PDAC risk rises with age, diabetes mellitus, and obesity, but whether this increased risk reflects a greater precancer burden is unknown, as previous studies assessed PanIN presence and grade. We aimed to quantify pancreatic composition and PanIN burden across the adult lifespan to identify demographics of donors carrying disproportionate precancer burden. Methods: We applied CODAvision, a deep-learning segmentation pipeline, to 410 high-quality pancreas sections from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) donors aged 21 to 70 years. We screened twenty-seven donor phenotypes against 14 compositional measures, applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. We further related tissue composition and donor phenotype to bulk gene expression in 281 donors to understand which demographics are associated with a compositional or transcriptional fingerprint. Results: PanIN was present in 83% of donors. Acinar proportion declined with age, offset by fat and stroma. Median PanIN burden did not change with age, though the fitted 90th percentile rose from 0.21% to 0.72% of exocrine tissue (uncorrected P=.002). The 39 sections (10%) with high-outlier PanIN burden came disproportionately from donors with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension and had greater stromal proportion and higher fibroblast and immune-cell densities. Both cell types were denser in peri-PanIN stroma than in the surrounding pancreatic parenchyma. PanIN abundance was associated with a gastric transcriptional signature including VSIG1, TFF1, and MUC5AC. Conclusions: Most donors carried little PanIN at any age, whereas high burden was concentrated in a minority of donors more likely to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and inflamed, fibrotic stroma. Because PanIN was present in most donors, its presence did not distinguish high-risk groups, whereas quantitative burden did, concentrating on the metabolic phenotypes already under consideration for pancreatic surveillance.

papers.title: Singular Value Decomposition for the Automated Analysis of NMR Fraction Libraries
papers.abstract: Identifying and quantifying molecular components of biological fluids offers great potential for the diagnosis of disease, detecting environmental contaminants, and process monitoring. The use of simple 1D 1H NMR spectra to accomplish this task offers advantages in terms of broad applicability and quantitative output. However, it also encounters obstacles in extracting individual components from complex superimposed spectra and in compound identification through comparison with limited database entries. Here, we present a new protocol that includes automatically separating component spectra using singular value decomposition (SVD) and matching them to database entries that carry both chemical shift and scalar coupling information. The procedure is illustrated by application to a fungal extract from Neurospora crassa that is chromatographically fractionated to form a two-dimensional spectral fraction library. Results are compared to a previous analysis that used a semi-manual curation of separated spectra followed by chemical shift matching.

papers.title: Resonant Recognition Model analysis of cGAS: conserved spectral frequencies and a divergent naked mole-rat phase signature
papers.abstract: Background: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) is a cytosolic DNA sensor with additional noncanonical nuclear functions, including suppression of homologous recombination (HR) in humans. In the naked mole-rat (NMR), cGAS instead promotes HR through a FANCI-RAD50-dependent mechanism, a functional reversal attributed to four C-terminal amino acid substitutions. Whether such functional divergence is reflected in primary-sequence-derived spectral features is unknown. Methods: We applied the Resonant Recognition Model (RRM) to cGAS sequences from fourteen mammals and to FANCI sequences from eight species. Sequences were converted to numerical series using EIIP values and analyzed by discrete Fourier transform; consensus spectra were generated by point-wise multiplication of individual power spectra. Phase differences between cGAS and FANCI were computed at frequencies of interest. Spectral amplitudes at the dominant shared frequency were correlated with body mass, lifespan, and lifespan-to-body-mass ratio. RRM frequencies were converted to electromagnetic wavelengths using the Cosic formulation ({lambda} = 201/f_RRM). Results: The cGAS consensus spectrum contained four prominent peaks (f = 0.0392, 0.0765, 0.2539, 0.4229), with 0.2539 dominant. Three FANCI peaks (0.04138, 0.2479, 0.4332) were close to cGAS peaks, and the combined cGAS+FANCI consensus retained peaks at 0.2539 and 0.04077. Spectral amplitude at f = 0.2539 correlated with body mass (r = 0.647, p < 0.05) and with lifespan-to-body-mass ratio (r = -0.677, p < 0.01); the NMR showed the lowest amplitude. Human cGAS-FANCI phase difference was 3.1297 rad, 0.0118 rad from opposition, satisfying the RRM interaction criterion; the NMR cGAS-FANCI pair gave 1.7319 rad, approximately {pi}/2, which does not satisfy the criterion. Conversion of the dominant frequency yielded a predicted wavelength of 792 nm (378.5 THz), in the near-infrared range. This prediction is testable in transparent vertebrate models: zebrafish respond to NIR light, and red-light pre-treatment has been reported to improve survival after lethal gamma irradiation in zebrafish embryos. Conclusions: RRM identifies conserved spectral features in cGAS consistent with a cGAS-FANCI relationship, and amplitude at the dominant frequency varies with life-history traits. The phase analysis does not support a direct interaction signature for NMR cGAS-FANCI, a negative result consistent with a chromatin-mediated mechanism. The cross-species phase comparisons suggest that NMR FANCI, not only NMR cGAS, may contribute to the distinctive interaction mode. The predicted 792 nm wavelength provides a concrete, experimentally accessible parameter for testing whether RRM-derived frequencies can modulate radiation resistance in a transparent vertebrate model. These results are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation.

papers.title: Genome-wide loss of chromatin accessibility coexists with selectively elevated RNA abundance in nutrient-starved U2OS cells
papers.abstract: Background Chromatin accessibility is widely used as a proxy for regulatory potential and is often interpreted together with RNA-seq to infer gene-regulatory responses. However, the quantitative relationship between chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance may become difficult to interpret, particularly under acute cellular stress. Metabolic challenges such as nutrient deprivation are known to induce extensive chromatin remodelling and transcriptional reprogramming, raising the question of whether changes in transcript abundance are directly governed by chromatin accessibility in these contexts. Clarifying this relationship is critical for interpreting epigenomic data under stress conditions, and requires careful distinction between Tn5 accessibility, relative steady-state RNA abundance and transcriptional output. Results We integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses in human U2OS osteosarcoma cells following 18 h of severe nutrient deprivation. We found that starvation was associated with a genome-wide reduction in accessibility and almost all significantly altered accessible regions showed reduced signal relative to actively growing cells. This decrease affected promoter- and enhancer-associated regions alike, including housekeeping-gene promoters and CTCF-motif sites. In contrast, RNA-seq revealed a more selective change in relative steady-state RNA abundance: only a minority of expressed genes were differentially regulated, and approximately 64% of differentially expressed genes showed increased relative RNA abundance. Changes in accessibility and transcript abundance were modestly correlated at promoters (Pearson r = 0.25) and weakly at enhancers (r = 0.10), and together explained only ~6% of the variance in transcript abundance changes. The relationship was graded: genes with the smallest promoter losses were about four times as likely to show increased RNA abundance as genes with the largest losses, independently of baseline promoter accessibility. Within-condition analyses similarly showed only modest relationships between promoter accessibility and RNA abundance in both actively growing and starved cells. Pathway-level analysis of mRNA abundance revealed the expected repression of biosynthetic and growth-related programmes, including ribosome biogenesis, translation and cellular growth, together with a less anticipated relative activation of stress-adaptive programmes, including extracellular matrix organisation, lipid and cholesterol metabolism, small GTPase signalling and developmental processes. For genes within these activated programmes, increased steady-state mRNA abundance was observed despite reduced ATAC-seq accessibility at associated regulatory regions. Exon-intron analyses of RNA-seq data indicated that these changes predominantly reflect altered RNA production. Metabolic labelling of nascent RNA at selected loci confirmed increased transcription of genes involved in adaptive programmes despite reduced promoter and enhancer accessibility, alongside with reduced production of biosynthetic transcripts and rRNA. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that chromatin accessibility and steady-state RNA abundance are only modestly coupled during severe nutrient deprivation, against a baseline of similarly modest promoter accessibility-abundance coupling. This underscores the limited ability of ATAC-seq accessibility to predict transcript abundance under this stress condition and supports a model in which chromatin accessibility acts as a permissive rather than deterministic layer of gene regulation. The selective induction of adaptive programmes, confirmed here at the level of RNA production, shows that transcriptional activation can occur despite genome-wide loss of ATAC-seq accessibility. Because ATAC-seq reports Tn5 accessibility rather than physical chromatin compaction, we interpret compaction as a plausible mechanistic model compatible with the current observations, which will require direct orthogonal validation.

papers.title: TileScope quantifies spatial gene expression relationships beyond colocalization
papers.abstract: Gene expression patterns within the same tissue region can exhibit similar correlation or enrichment, but still differ in their organization within regions and at their boundaries. We present TileScope, a framework for analysing genes and transcriptional programs within predefined tissue regions, their components and their contacts with neighbouring regions. TileScope combines regional enrichment, within-region correlation, cross-correlation over distance and expression differences near specific boundaries. Repeated spatial partitions and consensus aggregation show how these measurements depend on the grouping of spots or cells. Across 30 controlled constructions derived from glioblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma data representing ten spatial expression scenarios, combined measurements separated arrangements that individual statistics left ambiguous, including coincident patches, gradients and expression localised at region boundaries. In 30 human glioblastoma sections, TileScope distinguished shared regional enrichment from internal covariation and identified hypoxia-associated expression localised at region boundary despite negligible within-region correlation. In newly acquired Visium profiles of control and myeloid-targeted MCT1-knockout (KO) orthotopic GL261 mouse gliomas, proliferation and myeloid programs were enriched in tumour peripheries but showed opposite within-periphery-region correlations. Proliferation was higher near the tumour-facing boundary in both samples, whereas myeloid expression was higher near the tumour-facing boundary in the control and farther within periphery in the KO condition. Xenium applications on glioblastoma and breast cancer samples demonstrated feasibility with irregularly spaced individual cells and different regional annotations. TileScope provides spatially explicit descriptions of gene and program relationships, linking their organization within tissue compartments to their sensitivity to aggregation.

papers.title: Development and cross-cohort evaluation of a multimodal deep-learning model for ER, PR and HER2 status classification in breast cancer
papers.abstract: Background. Estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2 status guide systemic treatment in breast cancer. Multimodal models are rarely benchmarked against key biomarker molecular baselines or evaluated for cross-cohort calibration. We assessed incremental value, dependence on label-proximal HER2 transcripts, and transport of discrimination and calibration. Methods. A model combining whole-slide images, transcriptomes, age and stage was developed in TCGA-BRCA (1051 patients; ER/PR/HER2 analysis sets: 1001/998/1006) and evaluated in CPTAC-BRCA (120 patients; 118/113/95). CPTAC had been observed during earlier development and included 13 HER2-positive cases. Analyses included paired model comparisons, transcript removal, alternative loss functions and recalibration. Internal discrimination used pooled out-of-fold predictions; external discrimination used fold-mean estimates, with ensemble calibration reported separately. Internal calibration and macro-AUC uncertainty were interpreted as exploratory. Results. Internal AUCs were 0.943 for ER, 0.901 for PR, and 0.860 for HER2; external AUCs were 0.952, 0.937, and 0.918, respectively. External macro-AUC was 0.936 for the multimodal model and 0.957 for logistic regression using ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 (difference -0.021). Removal of the extended 29-transcript 17q12-q21 region changed HER2 AUC by -0.035 [-0.058 to -0.013] (95% CI) internally and by -0.042 [-0.089 to -0.007] externally relative to the baseline multimodal model. For external 15-model ensemble predictions, recalibrated HER2 expected calibration error (ECE) was 0.236, exceeding the ECE reference ceiling of 0.125, while calibration-in-the-large was -1.657 [-2.373 to -1.023] (profile-likelihood 95% CI), indicating systematic overprediction. ER and PR also showed overprediction. In paired fold-mean comparisons, HER2 ECE and Brier score favoured the three-transcript model (ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2). Conclusions. A multimodal deep-learning model achieved high discrimination across cohorts but did not demonstrate clear incremental value over a parsimonious three-transcript baseline, while cross-cohort calibration remained a substantial challenge. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating incremental value, calibration, and clinical utility alongside discrimination when assessing AI-based prediction models for medical use.

papers.title: DoAggregate: a pipeline for aggregation testing for rare-variant on a gene and pathway level
papers.abstract: Motivation Aggregation tests overcome the classical limitation of rare variant analysis in cohort study design. Choosing the right statistical test remains one of the biggest challenges. Existing tools fall short in offering a comprehensive solution that includes automatic data processing, testing across all genes, as well as exploration of broader genetic regions such as pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms. Most aggregation tests only report p-values and basic statistics, lacking in the presentation of cohort level statistics and comparison of results across whole genome or exome scales. Results We introduce DoAggregate, an innovative, scalable pipeline designed to address these challenges. DoAggregate enables users to perform aggregation tests across genes, pathways, and GO terms. It leverages Excalibur, an ensemble approach combining 36 distinct aggregation methods. The pipeline enhances data analysis by presenting over-representation analysis and aggregation results in detailed Excel sheets, complete with annotations and plots to facilitate nuanced interpretation and comparison. Applied to public exome data from the 1000 Genomes Project, DoAggregate tested 10,447 genes, 49 over-represented pathways and 36 over-represented GO terms in a single run, returning annotated, cohort-level results for each region. Availability and implementation DoAggregate source code, documentation and installation instructions as well as test data sets and results are freely available at https://github.com/boutrys/DoAggregate and released under the MIT license. The repository contains the serial implementation (R package), the parallel implementation for Slurm-based computer clusters and the web application.

papers.title: Integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of human cartilage reveals coordinated changes in fibronectin expression, splicing, and receptor signaling during osteoarthritis progression
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is defined by progressive loss of articular cartilage, but how chondrocytes change as the disease advances is unclear because most studies have focused on end-stage tissue. We profiled human knee articular cartilage across the full range of macroscopic OA grade, from young healthy to aged severe OA donors, by bulk RNA sequencing of 92 knees, single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 108,600 chondrocyte nuclei from 30 donors and single-nucleus multiome sequencing of 24 of these donors, treating grade as a continuous variable. With increasing grade, cartilage increased extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and remodeling genes, lost glucocorticoid-responsive, lipid-metabolic and antioxidant programs, and changed the splicing of a small set of ECM transcripts, led by the extra domain B (EDB) exon of fibronectin (FN1). Nine chondrocyte clusters were present in every disease stage and formed a continuum ordered by cartilage zone and hypertrophic differentiation, with PRG4+ superficial and COL10A1+ hypertrophic chondrocytes as the only distinct cell types at its ends and a pre-hypertrophic state between them. With grade, all clusters shared a response in which ECM production rose and homeostatic programs fell, and they differed in which of its components was strongest: ECM production in the superficial cells, the secretory pathway in the hypertrophic and CYTL1+ cells, and inflammatory signaling in the ANXA1+ and CRISPLD2+ cells. Inferred communication between chondrocytes was remodeled with stage. FN1 was induced in every cluster in excess of its fibril-assembly machinery, together with the fibronectin-cleaving protease HTRA1, and FN1 signaling shifted in receptor use from integrin 5{beta}1 toward CD44 and, less robustly, v{beta}8, accompanied by a rise in TGF-{beta}/SMAD response genes. In four early-OA donors, tenascin-C was already largely induced and the FN1 receptor shift from 5{beta}1 toward CD44 was partly present, whereas the rise of FN1 outside superficial chondrocytes, of FGF1 and of developmental and ossification programs came with progression. Chromatin accessibility changed in the same direction across clusters, with regions linked to FN1 opening and regions linked to ITGA5 closing. OA progression in human cartilage therefore appears to be a change of chondrocyte state that differs in emphasis along a zonal and hypertrophic continuum and includes changes in fibronectin regulation, production, processing, and receptor engagement.

papers.title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
papers.abstract: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

papers.title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
papers.abstract: textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

papers.title: PhenoMe: An interactive AI framework for interpretable, microscopy-driven phenotyping
papers.abstract: Extracting meaningful biological patterns from microscopy image datasets requires tools that quantitatively connect visual similarities and experimental context. Deep learning models, and in particular novel foundation models, have the capacity to translate images into high-dimensional embeddings that can better represent complex visual patterns. Using these complex representations analytically and linking them to experimental information, it is possible to build advanced exploratory and phenotyping capabilities. Here, we present PhenoMe, an open-source, model-agnostic framework to handle pretrained foundation model-derived image representations alongside quantitative image properties and experimental metadata. PhenoMe integrates multiple scriptable and interactive workflows for embedding space visualisation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, similarity-based comparison and retrieval of representative images for each phenotype, among others. It also supports correlation analyses that link the embedding structure to interpretable image properties. We demonstrate PhenoMe's capabilities on seven public microscopy datasets, ranging from cell painting assays, nanoscale synaptic images, drug-response analyses and dynamic cell-phenotyping. These case studies show how readily available image representations can support data contextualisation, curation and analysis. Through guided notebooks, reproducible configurations, extensible model wrappers and a napari plugin, PhenoMe makes representation-based microscopy exploration accessible to researchers without dedicated technical expertise. PhenoMe lays the groundwork for applying foundation models and representation learning to microscopy data analysis.
